sentence: Opioids such as morphine are prescription painkillers for severe pain; the NHS lists constipation and sleepiness as common side effects.
note: Morphine pages: prescription, severe pain; constipation and sleepiness common.

sentence: The NHS describes morphine as a strong opioid painkiller, available only on prescription and used for severe pain, such as after an operation or serious injury, or from cancer.
note: Morphine pages: strong opioid painkiller, prescription only, severe pain after operation/serious injury, cancer.

sentence: Constipation, feeling sick and sleepiness are the most common morphine side effects the NHS lists, and the chance of side effects is higher with a higher dose.
note: Side effects page: most common are constipation, feeling sick, drowsiness; higher dose, more chance of side effects.

sentence: The NHS says the body can become used to tramadol over time, so higher doses may gradually be needed, and that it is possible to become addicted.
note: Tramadol common questions: tolerance, higher doses gradually needed, possible to become addicted. Morphine page: addiction possible.

sentence: The NHS says morphine should not be stopped suddenly because withdrawal symptoms may follow, and that a doctor reduces the dose gradually over time.
note: Morphine page: 'Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly because you may get withdrawal symptoms. Your doctor will gradually reduce your dose over time.'

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for breathing difficulties or a seizure, NHS 111 can give urgent advice about side effects, and a GP may be a good place to start for help with drug addiction.
note: Side effects page: 999 for breathing difficulties or seizure; 111 for urgent advice. Getting-help page: GP may be a good place to start.

sentence: The NHS describes morphine as a strong opioid painkiller that is available only with a prescription.
note: Morphine pages: strong opioid painkiller; prescription only.

sentence: It is used to treat severe pain, such as pain after an operation or a serious injury, or pain from cancer or a heart attack.
note: About morphine: severe pain such as after operation, serious injury, cancer, heart attack.

sentence: The NHS also says it is used for longer-lasting pain when weaker painkillers no longer work.
note: About morphine: longer-lasting pain when weaker painkillers no longer work.

sentence: Morphine acts in the central nervous system and brain to stop pain signals reaching the rest of the body, and it also eases the anxiety and stress that pain produces.
note: About morphine: works in central nervous system and brain to block pain signals and reduce anxiety and stress caused by pain.

sentence: The NHS describes it as a controlled medicine and says that, because addiction is possible, the dose is reviewed so that a person takes only what is needed to control the pain.
note: About morphine: controlled medicine; addiction possible; dose reviewed to take only what is needed.

sentence: According to the NHS, morphine can be given in several ways, including as an injection into a vein, as tablets or liquid, and as slow-release forms.
note: About morphine: injection into a vein, tablets and liquid, slow-release forms.

sentence: An injection into a vein gives the quickest relief, working almost straight away.
note: About morphine: injection into a vein works almost straight away.

sentence: Tablets and liquid act more slowly than an injection, and slow-release forms take longer to start working but last longer.
note: About morphine: tablets/liquid slower; slow-release takes longer to start but lasts longer.

sentence: The NHS says the amount of pain a person has, rather than the stage of their illness, decides whether morphine is prescribed.
note: About morphine: pain level, not stage of illness, decides prescribing.

sentence: The NHS says the most common side effects of morphine are constipation, feeling sick and sleepiness.
note: Side effects: most common are constipation, feeling sick, drowsiness.

sentence: Dizziness, confusion, headaches and an itchy skin or rash can also occur.
note: Side effects: dizziness, confusion, headaches, itchy skin or rash.

sentence: The NHS says the higher the dose of morphine, the more chance of side effects.
note: Side effects: higher dose, more chance of side effects.

sentence: Morphine slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation, and the NHS says a laxative is likely to be needed to help prevent or treat it.
note: About morphine: slows digestion; side effects: likely to need a laxative.

sentence: Feeling sick should normally wear off after a few days, and the NHS says that taking the dose with a meal or snack helps.
note: Side effects: nausea wears off after a few days; meal or snack helps.

sentence: Drowsiness typically fades as the body adjusts, and the NHS says to speak to a doctor or pharmacist with any concerns.
note: Side effects: drowsiness fades as body adjusts; speak to doctor or pharmacist with concerns.

sentence: The NHS tramadol page says the body can become used to the medicine with long-term use, which means higher doses are gradually needed to get the same effect.
note: Tramadol common questions: body can become used to it; higher doses gradually needed.

sentence: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to tramadol, and it lists people with a history of addiction to alcohol, strong painkillers or recreational drugs among those who may not be able to take it.
note: Tramadol common questions: possible to become addicted; who can and cannot take: addiction to alcohol, strong painkillers or recreational drugs.

sentence: For morphine, the NHS says addiction is possible and that the dose is reviewed.
note: About morphine: addiction possible; dose reviewed.

sentence: NICE guidance on medicines associated with dependence links long-term treatment and higher doses taken long term with a greater risk of dependence.
note: NG215 evidence: long-term treatment is a risk factor for dependence, higher doses long term increase it.

sentence: NICE chronic pain guidance recommends against starting opioids for chronic primary pain.
note: NG193: recommends against starting opioid treatment for chronic primary pain.

sentence: The NHS says not to stop taking morphine suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms may follow.
note: Morphine page and common questions: if you stop suddenly you may get withdrawal symptoms.

sentence: It lists agitation, panic attacks, palpitations, sweating and restlessness as examples.
note: Morphine common questions list: agitation, panic attacks, palpitations, sweating, restlessness.

sentence: The NHS says a doctor will gradually reduce the dose over time.
note: Morphine page: Your doctor will gradually reduce your dose over time.

sentence: NICE says clinicians should explain the risk of stopping abruptly, and its guidance favours slow dose reduction, noting that the pace of safe withdrawal differs between people.
note: NG215: explain risk of abrupt discontinuation; slow reduction favoured; pace differs between people.

sentence: For questions about stopping, the NHS points to the prescriber or a pharmacist.
note: Side effects page: speak to doctor or pharmacist with concerns.

sentence: For tramadol, the NHS advises not drinking alcohol, because side effects such as feeling sleepy are more likely.
note: Tramadol common questions: alcohol; more likely to get side effects like feeling sleepy.

sentence: For morphine, the NHS says it may be best not to drink alcohol, because it may make a person feel sleepier or increase the risk of serious side effects.
note: Morphine: 'It may be best not to drink alcohol while taking morphine as it may make you feel more sleepy or increase the risk of serious side effects.'

sentence: The NHS says not to drive a car, ride a bike or use heavy tools or machinery if tramadol makes a person sleepy or dizzy, and gives similar advice for morphine when drowsy or dizzy.
note: Tramadol: do not drive, ride bike or use tools if sleepy; morphine: avoid driving if drowsy/dizzy.

sentence: The NHS also says that recreational drugs can raise the risk of serious side effects with tramadol.
note: Tramadol common questions: recreational drugs raise risk of serious side effects.

sentence: The NHS says serious side effects of morphine are uncommon, and include an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), slowed breathing and changes to vision.
note: Side effects page: serious effects uncommon; anaphylaxis, slowed breathing, visual changes.

sentence: It says to call 999 for breathing difficulties or a seizure, and also for signs of anaphylaxis such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue.
note: Side effects: 999 for breathing difficulties or seizure; morphine page: call 999 if lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell.

sentence: For urgent advice about side effects, the NHS points to NHS 111.
note: Side effects page: NHS 111 for urgent advice.

sentence: For help with drug addiction, the NHS says a GP may be a good place to start, as they can discuss the problem and help get a person into treatment.
note: Getting-help page: GP may be a good place to start; discuss problems and help into treatment.

sentence: The GP will usually refer to a local drug service, and the NHS adds that many drug treatment services accept self-referrals.
note: Getting-help page: usually refer to local drug service; many services accept self-referral.
